title: Broken Access Control: IDOR, CSRF and SSRF
oneLiner: Three ways an attacker uses access they shouldn't have: changing an ID in a URL, getting your browser to send a request for them, and getting the server to fetch internal addresses.
keyTakeaway: Access control has to be enforced on the server, for every request and every object: who is asking, and may they do this to this record? CSRF abuses the browser sending your cookies automatically, and is stopped by SameSite cookies and anti-CSRF tokens. SSRF abuses the server's network position, and is stopped by allowlisting destinations and checking the resolved IP address.
explanation:
Broken access control is the number one risk in the OWASP Top 10: the app correctly knows who you are (authentication) but doesn't correctly check what you may do (authorization). The simplest form is IDOR, an insecure direct object reference: the URL /api/invoices/1043 shows your invoice, and changing it to 1044 shows someone else's, because the server only checked that you were logged in. Hiding an admin button in the interface is the same mistake: anyone can send the request the button would have sent. The fix is a server-side check on every request, ideally in one shared place, that denies by default.

CSRF, cross-site request forgery, turns your own browser against you. Browsers attach a site's cookies to every request to that site, even when another page started it. A malicious page can therefore submit a hidden form to a site you're signed in to, and the request arrives with your session. Two defences work together: cookies marked SameSite=Lax or Strict, which browsers don't send on cross-site form posts, and an anti-CSRF token, a random value in each form that another site can't read. ASP.NET Core's antiforgery support adds the token for you.

SSRF, server-side request forgery, abuses features where the server fetches a URL for you: link previews, webhooks, "import from URL". The server sits inside the network, so an attacker can point it at addresses they can't reach themselves: internal admin pages, databases, or the cloud metadata service at 169.254.169.254, which can return the server's own cloud credentials. Filtering the URL text doesn't work, because the same address can be written many ways or hidden behind a DNS name. Resolve the name, check the actual IP against private, loopback and link-local ranges, connect to that IP, and best of all allow only known destinations. Try all three attacks below and switch the defences on.
